title: Scaling agent teams: reach the frontier at 30% of the cost
gist: Cohere's controlled study of coding-agent teams on ProgramBench finds teams beat solo agents by up to ~10 points at 3-7X the cost, but a strong lead delegating only planning to cheap workers reaches near-frontier reward (61.8% vs 63.2%) at $155 vs $510. The gains hinge on where agents are allocated and on how well the lead model delegates, varying sharply by model family.

themes.theme: Agent teams as a new inference-time scaling axis

insights.claim: Well-organized teams of coding agents outperform single agents on hard coding tasks, by up to ~10 percentage points on ProgramBench, but at 3-7X the cost, so the real question is how to make the extra compute count.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Multi-agent teams are a new way to spend inference compute; expect token demand to rise sharply for agentic coding, with cost-efficiency the differentiator.
insights.quote: The question is not whether more agents help, but how to make that additional compute count.

insights.claim: In a Sol-only comparison, a blocking agent team passed 61.8% of ProgramBench tests versus 52.1% for a solo agent with the same minimal prompt; a structured plan-implement-verify (PIV) prompt lifted the solo agent to 57.7% and the team to 63.1%, with all four Sol teams costing 4-7X their solo counterparts.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Prompt structure recovers roughly half of the team gain for a solo agent at far lower cost, so benchmark claims about multi-agent lift depend on solo baseline quality.
insights.locator: Teams outperform solo agents, at a cost

insights.claim: Teams of coding agents have moved from demos to large projects in the past year: sixteen Claude agents wrote a 100,000-line C compiler able to build the Linux kernel (~2,000 sessions, ~$20,000 API cost), Cursor agents wrote a million-line browser in about a week, and Bun was ported from Zig to Rust in 11 days with up to 64 Claude agents.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that agent swarms can produce large codebases, with API spend in the tens of thousands of dollars per project.

insights.claim: Factory's three-role team (orchestrator, implementer, validator) more than doubled a single agent's reward on rebuilding GDAL, but cost 14 times as much and took 13 times as long, showing how large the cost of teams can be.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Quality gains from multi-agent setups can come with order-of-magnitude cost and latency penalties.

insights.claim: The three well-known agent-team projects used different structures (peer agents claiming tasks through lock files, hierarchical planners delegating to hundreds of workers, fixed roles with one implementer, two adversarial reviewers and one fixer), so comparing them reveals little about which design choices mattered.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Argues for controlled experiments over anecdote when judging agent architectures.
insights.locator: Each of these teams produced working software

themes.theme: Allocate agents to the bottleneck: planning wins

insights.claim: Where agents are allocated matters more than how many: on ProgramBench, delegating only exploration and planning matched delegating all three stages (63.6% vs 63.2%) at half the cost ($249 vs $510), and was about twice as cost-efficient per added $100 as the next-best stage.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: The investable idea is that targeting compute at the true bottleneck beats brute-force agent count; efficiency tooling and task-aware orchestration are valuable.
insights.quote: Where you allocate agents matters more than how many you add.

insights.claim: Planning workers pay off on ProgramBench because the target program is a black box whose behavior must be discovered by running it; parallel planners each probe a different part of the interface, giving the lead a fuller picture before it writes the code.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Parallel exploration helps when specification discovery is the hard part, as in reverse-engineering or legacy migration.
insights.locator: The reason lies in the benchmark's design

insights.claim: When the specification is already provided, as in Commit0 with repo skeletons and unit tests, implementation rather than planning was the most effective stage to delegate in eight of ten team setups, though frontier models nearly saturate Commit0 (a solo agent passes every test on 12 of 16 tasks), so this is only suggestive.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: The best delegation stage depends on the task's bottleneck, so no universal agent-team recipe exists.
insights.locator: Commit0 shows the other side of this

insights.claim: Other reports are consistent: Factory's validator probes the reference program to build an executable definition of done before coding, and Carlini's C-compiler team got unstuck on the Linux kernel by using GCC as an oracle, so knowing what to build was the bottleneck.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Verifiable oracles and spec discovery recur as the unlock in successful agent builds.
insights.locator: Other works have reported related findings

insights.claim: A future lead that can detect where its own task is stuck could move workers to that stage without being told which stage to delegate, since the best stage varies by task (planning on ProgramBench, implementation on Commit0).
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Adaptive orchestration is a research direction that could change cost-efficiency of agent platforms.

insights.claim: A Sol lead coordinating 16 inexpensive Luna planning workers reaches 61.8% reward versus 63.2% for an all-Sol team delegating every stage, cutting cost from $510 to $155 (about 70% lower).
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: A heterogeneous model mix delivers near-frontier results at about a third of the price, a template for cost control in agent deployments and a pressure on premium-model pricing.
insights.quote: A strong lead with cheap workers delivers near-frontier performance at 70% lower cost.

insights.claim: With Sol as lead and Luna planning workers, the team gave up a few points versus the all-Sol team (60.5% vs 63.6%) but kept 47.5% of the all-Sol team's gain for only 13.9% of its extra cost, so each dollar bought more than three times as much reward.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Cheap-model tiers have outsized value as worker models in agentic stacks.

insights.claim: Lead quality cannot be bought back with cheap workers: holding Luna workers fixed, reward rose from 42.5% to 51.6% to 60.5% as the lead went from Luna to Terra to Sol, and a Terra lead with Luna workers (51.6%) still lagged a solo Sol agent (57.7%).
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Spend on the strongest model for the decision-making role; the controller is where frontier-model premiums are justified.

insights.claim: This matches Meta's meta-reasoning work, where a better controller scored 71.5% against 63.7% on ProgramBench with the same workers and budget, and the advantage widened as budget grew while simpler control leveled off.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Independent corroboration that decision-making models are the leverage point in agent systems.
insights.locator: This matches recent work from Meta

insights.claim: Models should be trained to lead: because models differed widely in how well they used a team, the authors suggest leading (delegating well, weighing conflicting reports, knowing when to wait) is a trainable skill that could extract more from the same workers.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Expect labs to market and train 'orchestrator' capability as a distinct model feature.

insights.claim: Planning teams improved with size, from 59.6% with two Luna workers to 61.8% with sixteen, because each planner ran the reference program about seven times regardless of team size, so total runs grew from 15 to 109 and reports from 17,000 to 75,000 characters.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Parallel information gathering scales cleanly, which favors workloads where extra workers add new information.

insights.claim: Implementation and verification workers peaked at about four and then slipped as more were added, because each implementer received a thinner plan slice (about 1,400 characters per worker with two vs 440 with sixteen) while the lead did not verify the combined program more often.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Adding implementers has diminishing and sometimes negative returns; coordination overhead is the limit.
insights.locator: Extra implementers added no such information

insights.claim: Letting agents message each other mostly produced upward reporting: 84% of messages in Sol PIV teams went from workers to the lead and peer messages averaged under one per task; reward did not change for Sol and Terra teams and Luna teams lost 4-7 points, partly because about half their send_message calls were malformed.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Peer-to-peer agent chat is not a free win in delegation-style harnesses; weaker models can be hurt by it.

insights.claim: Communication may help in other settings: Park et al. found five communicating agents with a shared goal and workspace matched the best of 33 independent agents on ARC-AGI-3, with 'verified progress sharing' as the key ingredient, and Microsoft's Agensh reports cooperation emerging in large flat teams.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Self-organizing agent teams remain an open area; track results on shared-goal tasks.

insights.claim: A team of thousands of agents working for weeks would likely outgrow what any single lead can track, raising the open question of whether real coordination emerges with scale or must be trained, which the authors see as central to scaling inference.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: The orchestration layer, not model count, may be the next scaling bottleneck for agent workforces.

insights.claim: Teams helped GPT-5.6 (up to +6.9 points over its best solo agent) and Claude Opus 4.8 (+5.9 with PIV and an asynchronous lead), but Claude Opus 4.7 rarely delegated (at most 1.3 times per task) and gained little, while Claude Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 3.7 Flash delegated readily but gained nothing; results are single runs with noise of about 5 points.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Agentic delegation skill varies sharply even within a model family, a useful lens when comparing frontier models for coding-agent products.
insights.locator: How other models use a team

insights.claim: Two things must go right for a team to help: the lead must choose to delegate and it must make good use of what comes back; Opus 4.7 failed the first, Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 3.7 Flash the second.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Provides a diagnostic for evaluating whether a model is ready to lead agent teams.
insights.quote: Two things have to go right for a team to help.
insights.locator: How other models use a team

insights.claim: Models differ in their output style: GPT-5.6 rebuilt most programs in Python (70-93% of submissions) regardless of the original language, Claude models reimplemented in the original language (72-90%), and Claude Opus 4.8 and the Gemini Flash models spread programs over a median of 5-11 files versus 1-3 for GPT-5.6.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Model-specific coding habits affect maintainability and fidelity, which matters for migration and rewrite use cases.
insights.locator: The models also structured their programs differently

insights.claim: Claude Opus 5 on the 30-task subset was stopped after eight trial tasks all hit an eight-hour timeout, each costing roughly $500, about 15 times what an Opus 4.8 team spent per task.
insights.speaker: Cohere
insights.so_what: Newer frontier models in team mode can be dramatically more expensive per task, a cost risk for agentic deployment.
